newsitem.title: USA: Foreign interests buy White House access - Dole.
newsitem.headline: Foreign interests buy White House access - Dole.

text.p: Saying foreign interests were trying to buy White House access through big donations to the Democratic party, Republican Bob Dole on Sunday called for banning all campaign contributions from non-citizens.

In a hard-hitting speech at Daniel Webster College here, the Republican presidential nominee also took on the AFL-CIO labour union, which is funding a $35 million advertising campaign to elect Democrats to Congress, saying lawmakers must bar use of compulsory union dues for political purposes.

The Democratic National Committee (DNC) is under fire for accepting hundreds of thousands of dollars in questionable campaign contributions from individuals with ties to the Lippo Group, an Indonesian real estate and banking conglomerate.

DNC officials on Friday removed fundraiser John Huang, who formerly worked for the Lippo Group, and asked the Federal Election Commission to investigate charges about some of the donations he brought in. Democrats have also been criticised for a fundraiser held at a Buddhist temple in California.

"Foreign aid has finally reached America, it's reaching the United States now, it's all going to the Democratic National Comittee," Dole said, charging foreign contributors were trying to buy access to the White House.
"We simply cannot allow the influence of any American to be outweighed by foreign money ... if you're not eligible to vote, you shouldn't be allowed to make a contribution," he said.

Dole promised if elected he would appoint a bipartisan commission to recommend an overhaul of campaign finance reform laws including abolishing so-called "soft money" -- big bucks contributions to political parties to get around strict limits on giving to individual candidates.
He also made a vague promise to rein in the influence of political action committees.
President Bill Clinton's re-election campaign responded that "it's a little late and disingenuous for Bob Dole to promote campaign finance reform."

"Bob Dole has made a career opposing meaningful campaign finance reform," said Joe Lockhard, spokesman for Clinton's and Vice President Al Gore's re-election committee. "It's too bad that Senator Bob Dole's record doesn't match candidate Dole's rhetoric."
Promises to overhaul finance laws are a staple of political campaigns, but have produced few concrete results in recent years.

President Bill Clinton and House of Representatives Speaker Newt Gingrich, appearing together in New Hampshire in 1995, recommended the type of bipartisan panel Dole is suggesting. It never happened. Instead campaign finance reform died in Congress and both parties have stepped up fundraising.
The speech reflected Dole's recent campaign strategy of attacking Clinton's ethics as he tries to catch up in the polls, with the Nov. 5 elections fast approaching.

Clinton, who narrowly won New Hampshire in the 1992 elections, is running far ahead of Dole in what should be a solidly Republican state. Recent polls have shown Dole lagging by double-digit margins in the state and Clinton may sweep the Northeast.

Dole has never received a friendly welcome in New Hampshire -- he lost the state's pivotal primary -- and Sunday was no exception. Dole's campaign plane landed in the midst of a raging storm that tossed it back and forth so hard some overhead panels opened, releasing emergency air bags.
From New Hampshire, Dole will travel to Delaware for a rally before returning to Washington. On Monday and Tuesday he will visit Michigan, another must-win state where he lags badly in the polls.
